Opening

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · LESSON A · 2 MINUTES

Spherical Bodies: Shape Evidence

Learning objective

I can compare a disc and a sphere, then use more than one piece of evidence about the shapes of space bodies.

Success looks like

  • Distinguish a flat disc from a three-dimensional sphere.
  • Keep viewpoints and distance consistent in a comparison.
  • Use evidence and a limitation to describe Earth, Sun and Moon as approximately spherical.

Two mystery objects look circular from the front. What extra observation would distinguish them?

Two separate lessons

A · Explore and explain · 40 minutes

B · Spherical Bodies: World Shape Lab · 40 minutes

Stop after Lesson A. Lesson B has its own start and exit.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Choose one route; equivalent science evidence does not require a written conversion.

Arrival

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · LESSON A · 5 MINUTES

Four clues to start

Choose a route. Today’s responses decide the help you use. No previous worksheet is needed.

Supported · 4 questions

1. Flat or solid

Point to ball for a three-dimensional object.

Help beside the question
A flat circle has no thickness in the ideal drawing.

Answer guidance

Answer: Ball.

2. One view

A shape looks circular from the front. Must it be a sphere?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. A disc can look circular too.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

3. Change the view

Choose narrow or still a wide circle for an edge-on card.

Help beside the question
Turn the card sideways.

Answer guidance

Answer: Narrow.

4. Fair comparison

Should you compare the ball close up and the disc far away?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Keep distance the same.

Answer guidance

Answer: No; use the same distance.

Standard · 4 questions

1. Flat or solid

Which is three-dimensional: a ball or a drawn circle?

Help beside the question
A solid has depth.

Answer guidance

Answer: The ball.

2. One view

A shape looks circular from the front. Must it be a sphere?

Help beside the question
A disc can look circular too.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

3. Change the view

What happens to a card disc’s outline when it is turned edge-on?

Help beside the question
Look along its thin edge.

Answer guidance

Answer: It looks very narrow.

4. Fair comparison

Should you compare the ball close up and the disc far away?

Help beside the question
Keep distance the same.

Answer guidance

Answer: No; use the same distance.

Stretch · 4 questions

1. Flat or solid

Which is three-dimensional: a ball or a drawn circle?

Help beside the question
Use an accurate science word. A solid has depth.

Answer guidance

Answer: The ball.

2. One view

Why is one circular photograph not enough to distinguish a disc from a sphere?

Help beside the question
Two different objects can have the same outline.

Answer guidance

Answer: Both can look circular from a particular viewpoint; more evidence is needed.

3. Change the view

What happens to a card disc’s outline when it is turned edge-on?

Help beside the question
Use an accurate science word. Look along its thin edge.

Answer guidance

Answer: It looks very narrow.

4. Fair comparison

Name two controls for a fair viewpoint comparison.

Help beside the question
Distance and viewing angle.

Answer guidance

Answer: Same viewing distance and same named angles for both objects.

I do

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · LESSON A · 7 MINUTES

Watch, predict, explain

Predict, model, explain

I compared the same views. The outline changed / stayed similar, which supports ___.

Make a prediction. Change one view, then use a label to explain what you notice.

Both the flat disc and the ball have a circular outline from the front.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Use front (0°), oblique (45°) and edge-on (90°): a quarter-turn is 90°, not the oblique view. The sphere is an ideal model; real bodies have surface features and Earth is slightly flattened. The Moon’s outer limb is curved; its light–dark boundary can look straight at quarter phase. A classroom model alone is not proof about Earth.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Front · 0°
Both the flat disc and the ball have a circular outline from the front.

08–16 seconds · Oblique · 45°
The disc looks oval. The ball still has a circular outline.

16–24 seconds · Edge-on · 90°
A quarter-turn presents the disc’s thin edge; the ball’s outline stays circular.

24–32 seconds · Combine evidence
The model helps interpret space observations. It is not itself a photograph or proof of Earth’s shape.

Read the card clues

Disc front: The front outline is circular.

Disc edge: The edge-on outline is narrow.

Ball views: The ball’s outline is circular in three views.

Compare views: The changing disc outline helps distinguish it from a sphere.

One photo proves all: One circular outline could belong to a disc or a sphere.

Perfectly smooth Earth: A ball model omits mountains and Earth’s slight flattening.

Supplied resources · read or print

Real-world evidence · reading cards

E1 · Earth

NASA describes Earth as a globe, with a small equatorial bulge. Spacecraft observations let people examine more than one part and viewpoint. This is a paraphrased reading card, not an actual photograph.

E2 · Moon and Sun

NASA’s solar-system material describes these bodies as broadly spherical. Drawings in this pack are explanatory diagrams, not measured photographs or scale models.

E3 · Compare the strength

One circular outline is compatible with more than one shape. Use multiple observations and reliable sources rather than treating one classroom model as proof.

Source route

Read the named NASA sources in the Teacher Pack. Point to one sentence you used, then state what it supports.

Use the evidence yourself

Supported · use one response mode

1. Match views

Match disc and ball to the supplied edge-on pictures.

Help: A thin edge belongs to the disc.

2. Use evidence

Complete: “At 90° the disc looks ___.”

Help: Choose narrow.

3. Make a careful claim

Choose approximately spherical for Earth.

Help: Use the evidence summaries.

Standard · use one response mode

1. Match views

Label the two objects at 0°, 45° and 90°.

Help: 45° is oblique; 90° is edge-on.

2. Use evidence

Compare two observations in a because sentence.

Help: State what changed.

3. Make a careful claim

Explain why one circular picture is not enough.

Help: A disc can look circular.

Stretch · use one response mode

1. Match views

Predict each outline and explain the geometric difference.

Help: A disc has very little depth.

2. Use evidence

Distinguish the observation from the interpretation in a comparison.

Help: I observed… This supports…

3. Make a careful claim

Combine the model with space evidence and name a limit.

Help: The classroom ball is not real Earth evidence.

Exit

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · LESSON A · 2 MINUTES

Two small checks

Supported · 2 questions

1. Distinguish

Which becomes narrow edge-on: disc or sphere?

Help beside the question
Compare the 90° view.

Answer guidance

Answer: Disc.

2. Careful wording

Why say Earth is approximately spherical?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. It is not an ideal perfectly smooth ball.

Answer guidance

Answer: Earth has surface features and is slightly flattened.

Standard · 2 questions

1. Distinguish

Describe one observation that separates a disc from a sphere.

Help beside the question
Compare edge-on outlines.

Answer guidance

Answer: An edge-on disc becomes narrow; a sphere keeps a circular outline.

2. Careful wording

Why say Earth is approximately spherical?

Help beside the question
It is not an ideal perfectly smooth ball.

Answer guidance

Answer: Earth has surface features and is slightly flattened.

Stretch · 2 questions

1. Distinguish

Describe one observation that separates a disc from a sphere.

Help beside the question
Use an accurate science word. Compare edge-on outlines.

Answer guidance

Answer: An edge-on disc becomes narrow; a sphere keeps a circular outline.

2. Careful wording

Give an evidence statement and its limit, without claiming a single image proves a sphere.

Help beside the question
Use multiple observations.

Answer guidance

Answer: Space observations from different viewpoints support a near-sphere; one circular view alone is insufficient.

Spherical Bodies: World Shape Lab

Arrival, investigation, checking and refining total 32 minutes. Then review the evidence for four minutes and complete two exit checks in four minutes.

Supported · 4 questions

1. View angles

Which view is a quarter-turn from front: 45° or 90°?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. A full turn is 360°.

Answer guidance

Answer: 90°.

2. Predict the disc

At 45°, choose oval or a perfect wide circle for a disc.

Help beside the question
It is slanted.

Answer guidance

Answer: Oval.

3. Evidence row

The ball looks circular at 0°, 45° and 90°. What does that support?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Use sphere-like.

Answer guidance

Answer: A sphere-like shape.

4. Beyond models

Name a source of evidence about the real Earth beyond our classroom ball.

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Think of spacecraft.

Answer guidance

Answer: Space observations / images from different viewpoints.

Standard · 4 questions

1. View angles

Which view is a quarter-turn from front: 45° or 90°?

Help beside the question
A full turn is 360°.

Answer guidance

Answer: 90°.

2. Predict the disc

Predict the outline of a flat disc at 45°.

Help beside the question
It is between front and edge-on.

Answer guidance

Answer: An oval / ellipse.

3. Evidence row

The ball looks circular at 0°, 45° and 90°. What does that support?

Help beside the question
Use sphere-like.

Answer guidance

Answer: A sphere-like shape.

4. Beyond models

Name a source of evidence about the real Earth beyond our classroom ball.

Help beside the question
Think of spacecraft.

Answer guidance

Answer: Space observations / images from different viewpoints.

Stretch · 4 questions

1. View angles

Which view is a quarter-turn from front: 45° or 90°?

Help beside the question
Use an accurate science word. A full turn is 360°.

Answer guidance

Answer: 90°.

2. Predict the disc

Predict the outline of a flat disc at 45°.

Help beside the question
Use an accurate science word. It is between front and edge-on.

Answer guidance

Answer: An oval / ellipse.

3. Evidence row

Does “circular in three views” establish a perfectly smooth planet?

Help beside the question
Outline is not every surface feature.

Answer guidance

Answer: No. It supports a broadly spherical shape, not perfect smoothness.

Workshop

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · LESSON B · 20 MINUTES

Gather and use evidence

Use a large clean ball and a stiff card disc with rounded edges. Hold at the same distance; do not use sharp skewers. Point to the supplied views or direct an adult instead. Never look at the Sun.

4 min · Predict the three named views.
20 min · Compare the ball and disc at the same distance; record all six outlines. Then read the space-evidence summary.
2 min · Check that 90°, not 45°, is the quarter-turn.
6 min · Explain which shape matches the outline pattern; state a limit.
ViewpointDisc outlineBall outline
Front · 0°Predict, then observePredict, then observe
Oblique · 45°Predict, then observePredict, then observe
Edge-on · 90°Predict, then observePredict, then observe

Supported route

Match front and edge-on outline cards; direct an adult to position each object. Explain one contrast by pointing.

Standard route

Record all six observations. Combine the outline pattern with the NASA evidence summary to support approximately spherical bodies.

Stretch route

Record six observations and controls. Explain why multiple viewpoints are stronger than one front view and why a model alone cannot establish Earth’s shape.

Shape-evidence decisions

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Check one piece of evidence

Check one piece of evidence

Did both objects use the same distances and viewing angles? Have you recorded outlines rather than simply writing “sphere”?

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Disc: circular at 0°, oval at 45°, narrow at 90°. Ideal ball: circular outline at all three views. Real space observations support near-spherical Earth, Moon and Sun; a small classroom ball does not itself establish their shape.

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can compare a disc and a sphere, then use more than one piece of evidence about the shapes of space bodies.

Key words

sphere — a three-dimensional ball shape

disc — a flat circular shape

viewpoint — where an observer looks from

evidence — observations that support an explanation

approximately — close to, but not perfectly

Remember

  • A circle in one view does not prove a sphere.
  • A disc becomes narrow when viewed edge-on.
  • A sphere keeps a circular outline from different directions.
  • Space observations support approximately spherical Earth, Sun and Moon.

Success looks like

  • Distinguish a flat disc from a three-dimensional sphere.
  • Keep viewpoints and distance consistent in a comparison.
  • Use evidence and a limitation to describe Earth, Sun and Moon as approximately spherical.

TA Brief

Current stage

Current stage:

Preparation and access

Use a large clean ball and a stiff card disc with rounded edges. Hold at the same distance; do not use sharp skewers. Point to the supplied views or direct an adult instead. Never look at the Sun.

Scientific care

Use front (0°), oblique (45°) and edge-on (90°): a quarter-turn is 90°, not the oblique view. The sphere is an ideal model; real bodies have surface features and Earth is slightly flattened. The Moon’s outer limb is curved; its light–dark boundary can look straight at quarter phase. A classroom model alone is not proof about Earth.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

Name: ____________________

Four checks. Point, speak, sign, draw, write or direct an adult.

1. Flat or solid

Which is three-dimensional: a ball or a drawn circle?

Help: Use an accurate science word. A solid has depth.

2. One view

Why is one circular photograph not enough to distinguish a disc from a sphere?

Help: Two different objects can have the same outline.

3. Change the view

What happens to a card disc’s outline when it is turned edge-on?

Help: Use an accurate science word. Look along its thin edge.

4. Fair comparison

Name two controls for a fair viewpoint comparison.

Help: Distance and viewing angle.

Arrival answers · A · Stretch

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Lesson A · Stretch

1. Flat or solid

Which is three-dimensional: a ball or a drawn circle?

The ball.

2. One view

Why is one circular photograph not enough to distinguish a disc from a sphere?

Both can look circular from a particular viewpoint; more evidence is needed.

3. Change the view

What happens to a card disc’s outline when it is turned edge-on?

It looks very narrow.

4. Fair comparison

Name two controls for a fair viewpoint comparison.

Same viewing distance and same named angles for both objects.

Evidence cards

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Read a clue, choose a group, then explain. Cut apart or point; no cutting is required.

Disc front

The front outline is circular.

Disc edge

The edge-on outline is narrow.

Ball views

The ball’s outline is circular in three views.

Compare views

The changing disc outline helps distinguish it from a sphere.

One photo proves all

One circular outline could belong to a disc or a sphere.

Perfectly smooth Earth

A ball model omits mountains and Earth’s slight flattening.

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Lesson B · Supported

Name: ____________________

Four checks. Point, speak, sign, draw, write or direct an adult.

1. View angles

Which view is a quarter-turn from front: 45° or 90°?

Help: Point, choose or say. A full turn is 360°.

2. Predict the disc

At 45°, choose oval or a perfect wide circle for a disc.

Help: It is slanted.

3. Evidence row

The ball looks circular at 0°, 45° and 90°. What does that support?

Help: Point, choose or say. Use sphere-like.

4. Beyond models

Name a source of evidence about the real Earth beyond our classroom ball.

Help: Point, choose or say. Think of spacecraft.

Answers · A · Standard

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Lesson A · Standard

Four-question arrival

1. Flat or solid: The ball.

2. One view: No.

3. Change the view: It looks very narrow.

4. Fair comparison: No; use the same distance.

Two-check exit

1. Distinguish: An edge-on disc becomes narrow; a sphere keeps a circular outline.

2. Careful wording: Earth has surface features and is slightly flattened.

Staff · feedback and access

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Audience and response

The lesson teacher is the named adult audience. Hear or read the pupil’s own science response. A click, downloaded file or completed box is not evidence that a request was heard.

Respond within the existing task

Offer reading help, fewer cards at once, clearer labels, an adult-directed model or additional thinking time. Say what can and cannot change, then check whether the adjustment helped.

No additional pupil artefact

A response can be spoken, pointed, signed, drawn or written. Do not require a separate Lundy record, signature or written conversion of an oral response.

An optional pupil-owned note such as “What I said, and what it changed” may be used in existing work. It is not a requirement. If scribing, keep the pupil’s own words; the adult is an audience, not a verifier.

Keep assessment honest

Use current school recording practice and unit criteria separately. This pack does not certify an award. Do not infer a policy code from automated checking or a download.
